transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-17 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Tasha (Redwood SE), Marcus (CTO), Priya (Lead ML), Daniel (Product), Leila (Infra), plus an intern

Auto-summary (auto):
Auric exploring open-model path for chat + tool-calling to enrich search results (internal product AuricFinder). Primary concerns: long-context support (10k+ tokens), multilingual (FR/AR/EN), data residency for EU clients, and private vs dedicated hosting tradeoffs. Agreed to run bench with sample prompts and infra team.

Topics (auto):
- Model selection: open vs closed models
- Context length and KV cache behavior
- Tool-calling (internal search API + DB lookups)
- Deployment: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS

Questions (auto):
- Can Redwood host in a Swiss/EU region for data residency?
- How does KV cache and prefix caching behave for 20k token conversations?

--- Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription may include errors) ---
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Marcus, do you want to kick with a quick context on Auric's use case?
[00:10] Marcus: Yeah thanks. So we run AuricFinder which is an internal search + summarization layer over customer documents. We're trying to add conversational capabilities and tool-calls to enrich results, so basically call out to our search API to fetch pieces, then ask the model to synthesize.
[00:26] Priya: And to add, we have long documents, legal and medical snippets. We need stable behaviour with at least 12k token context, ideally 20k for a lot of cases. Also multilingual: French and Arabic are important for EU and MENA customers.
[00:40] Tasha: Great, that helps. Quick clarifying question — are you thinking Hosted first or do you need Private from day one for compliance?
[00:47] Daniel: Product wants fast iteration, so Hosted for evaluation would be ideal. But legal and some enterprise customers will require EU residency and sometimes customer-managed keys. So we need to know where Dedicated vs Private becomes necessary.
[01:02] Evan: Totally. We typically recommend starting Hosted to iterate quickly — you can pick model variants and test. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and SLOs, and Private gives the VPC + KMS controls.
[01:14] Leila: For the EU residency question, can Redwood host in Switzerland or a specific EU region? 
[01:19] Tasha: Yes, we have region options; for Private deployments we can set the control plane and inference in EU regions. For Hosted we also offer EU region endpoints — we'll share the region list and certs.
[01:30] Marcus: Cool. On models: what open models do you see doing well for 20k context and tool-calling? We've tried a few and hit instability on long summaries.
[01:40] Tasha: So there are a couple of modern open families that have long-context variants. Some issues to watch — kernel selection and KV cache management matter because when you push >8k tokens the runtime will choose different kernels and batching behavior changes. We support models with native long-context optimizations and also patched variants.
[01:56] Priya: When you say KV cache, do you mean the attention cache? We've seen "KV cash" in some transcripts — sorry, my phone autocorrect. How does Redwood handle prefix caching so we don't re-send the whole convo each time?
[02:09] Tasha: Good question. We do prefix/KV caching so common prefixes or system prompts can be reused across requests. For very long contexts we chunk and maintain the KV cache on GPU memory; on dedicated and private deployments you can pin cache sizes and GC policies. On Hosted we recommend a hybrid approach: persistent KV for session-level prompts plus streaming for fresh context.
[02:30] Speaker 1 (intern): Is there a limit on how many sessions you can cache concurrently?
[02:35] Tasha: It depends on capacity; with dedicated pools you get more predictable concurrent caches. We'll include a sizing example in the benchmark doc.
[02:44] Marcus: Ok, about tool-calling: we want the model to call our AuricFinder API for relevant docs and then produce a user-facing synthesis. Does Redwood support structured tool outputs and function calling?
[02:56] Evan: Yes — Redwood supports function/tool calling patterns and structured outputs. You can register tools (APIs) and the runtime can route or sandbox calls. Note that when calling external tools you also need to think about latencies — if your search API is slow, you'll see end-to-end latency go up, so caching the search results or async tool calls are common patterns.
[03:15] Priya: We also want to rerank search hits with embeddings. Can Redwood host our embedding models or do we use Redwood's embedding endpoints?
[03:24] Tasha: We support embeddings as part of the API; customers can use Redwood-hosted embedding models or bring-your-own model in Dedicated/Private if you need data isolation. There's also a recommendation engine for quantized embedding models to reduce cost.
[03:36] Marcus: Latency vs cost — what's the tradeoff on Dedicated? We looked at H100 vs A100 choices for throughput.
[03:45] Tasha: Dedicated allows you to choose instance classes; H100 gives better throughput per GPU for large-context variants but costs more. We provide cost/performance profiles from our model catalog; for many workloads a quantized A100 config hits a good middle ground. We'll include expected tokens/sec and p99 latencies for similar customers.
[04:02] Daniel: On the security side, we need SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integration. Also audit logs are a must.
[04:11] Evan: Redwood has SOC2, SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit logs. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. We'll attach the security compliance docs.
[04:22] Leila: Any gotchas for ephemeral GPU pools and log retention? We want to ensure logs are retained for 12 months for audits.
[04:29] Tasha: That’s configurable — Hosted has default retention windows but enterprise plans can extend retention. Private gives you full control.
[04:35] Marcus: Back to model behaviour: we need deterministic-ish outputs for regulatory workflows and to be able to detect regressions. How does Redwood help with evals and rollouts?
[04:46] Tasha: Redwood Optimize provides prompt set linked evals, regression alerts, and rollout controls (canary, A/B, auto-fallback). You can pin model versions and push safe rollouts. We can also integrate your test harness into our eval pipeline.
[04:58] Priya: Good. For benchmarking, what should we measure? We had a rough list: cold-start latency, p99, tokens/sec, memory pressure under 20k tokens, tool-call round-trips. Anything else?
[05:11] Tasha: Also measure quality metrics — hallucination rate on designated prompt set, rerank accuracy using your labels, and cost-per-query under various batching settings. We'll add suggested thresholds.
[05:22] Evan: Quick practical note — for the pilot we usually recommend 1) pick 2 open models (one LLM with long-context, one smaller fallback), 2) run a 2-week bench across representative prompts, 3) do a canary integration with 1% of real traffic.
[05:36] Marcus: Timeline-wise that's feasible. Procurement and legal will need security docs early.
[05:40] Evan: We'll send the security packet after this call.
[05:44] Daniel: One odd question — we have partners in MENA that need Arabic dialect support. Any data on open model performance on Arabic conversational tasks?
[05:54] Tasha: Some of the open families have multilingual fine-tuned variants; quality varies. We'll share a small study and recommend specific models that do better for Arabic and French. Also, you might want to consider few-shot priming and retrieval-augmented generation to improve factuality.
[06:10] Priya: About tool safety — can we sandbox tools to avoid accidental PII leakage?
[06:15] Tasha: Yes, we can route tool calls through an isolation layer and optionally scrub responses; with Private you can host the tool runner inside your VPC for additional controls.
[06:24] Marcus: For the bench, we'll provide three datasets: legal, medical, and customer support logs (anonymized). We'll need guidance for creating the prompt sets.
[06:33] Evan: Great — Priya, you'll send those datasets and prompt examples. We'll pair Tasha with your infra folks for the benchmark.
[06:39] Leila: Network-wise, our infra is behind a strict egress policy — we'll need to test connectivity and maybe use a private peering for Dedicated.
[06:47] Tasha: We can support VPC peering and private links on Dedicated/Private. We'll include network diagrams and requirements.
[06:54] Daniel: Any documentation link for function calling schema and examples?
[06:58] Evan: Yes, we'll share a short dev quickstart and a sample repo with tool-calling patterns; also a demo we can run in 30 minutes.
[07:06] Marcus: On costs: can you ballpark monthly for a pilot (medium throughput, 200k tokens/day) on Hosted vs Dedicated?
[07:14] Evan: We'll put numbers in the pricing spreadsheet but rough back-of-envelope: Hosted pilot is generally cheaper upfront; Dedicated has a commitment but becomes cheaper at scale. We'll show both scenarios.
[07:25] Priya: One more — regression detection: do you store embeddings/outputs so we can diff?
[07:31] Tasha: We can retain request/response traces and embeddings depending on retention policy; for Private you get full control. We also integrate with Redwood Optimize to continuously compare model outputs on canonical prompts.
[07:44] Speaker 1 (intern): Quick pedantic point — how do you measure p99?
[07:47] Tasha: We measure end-to-end p99 across requests including tool-call latencies when instrumented, and also tokenize-level generation latency.
[07:56] Evan: Ok, last bit — success criteria for pilot? Marcus?
[08:00] Marcus: For exec: 1) 15% lift in retrieval relevance, 2) p99 < 1.5s for small queries and < 5s for long-context synth requests in canary, 3) no major security blockers for EU customers.
[08:14] Evan: Sounds good — we'll align the benchmark to those metrics.

--- Closing / Recap ---
[08:20] Evan: Recap: Redwood to share pricing, region list and security docs; SE to prepare benchmark checklist; Auric to send datasets and prompt sets; schedule bench with infra next week.
[08:33] Marcus: Thanks, look forward to the benchmark.
[08:36] Evan: Thanks all.

--- End transcript (approx) ---

Notes: transcription occasionally labels audience chatter as 'Speaker 1'. Some technical terms transcribed imperfectly (e.g., H100/A100 conflations, "KV cash" instead of KV cache).
